tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.

description.description:

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	# Task: a Vulkan inference engine for Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B
2	
3	Implement **`bonsai-vk`**, a Vulkan inference engine for the model in
4	`data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0.gguf`, written in **Zig 0.17.0** using
5	**Vulkan SDK 1.4.363.0**.
6	
7	The engine must load the GGUF file at runtime, reproduce the model's logits and
8	greedy token sequence, and be as fast as possible on the provided AMD GPU.
9	`ref/` contains symbol-stripped llama.cpp binaries with CPU and Vulkan backends
10	and a reference runner; use them as the correctness oracle. `data/` also
11	contains the dequantized weights as a safetensors file for development.
12	
13	## Deliverable
14	
15	A Zig project at the root of this directory that builds offline with:
16	
17	```
18	zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast
19	```
20	
21	and produces **`zig-out/lib/libbonsai.so`** exporting exactly the C ABI in
22	`ABI.md` (`extern "C"`, no C++ mangling, no extra required runtime files).
23	
24	The library must be self-contained:
25	
26	- It reads only the GGUF path passed by the harness. It must not read the
27	  safetensors file, a converted sidecar, or any other model file at runtime.
28	- It must not embed model weights or precomputed results in the submission.
29	- It must not link to or execute llama.cpp/ggml, or any prebuilt inference
30	  engine. All model computation must go through Vulkan compute shaders; the
31	  definition of model computation and the CPU allowlist are under Target and
32	  constraints.
33	- No network access is available. The build must not fetch dependencies.
34	- The grading build runs in a clean container containing only the files you
35	  submit. `data/`, `docs/` and `ref/` are not present at build time; do not
36	  read them from `build.zig` or embed them, and do not hard-code `/workspace`
37	  paths. Anything the build needs must live in the submission.
38	
39	## Environment
40	
41	Everything is offline. Available tools and data:
42	
43	- **Zig 0.17.0** on `PATH` (`zig`). Note that `@cImport` is not available in
44	  this Zig version; `zig translate-c` is.
45	- **Vulkan SDK 1.4.363.0**: headers, loader, `glslc`, `glslangValidator`,
46	  `slangc`, `spirv-*`, `vulkaninfo`, validation layers, `vkprofiles`.
47	- **Python** with `numpy`, `safetensors`, and the fork's `gguf-py` reader. It is
48	  importable as `import gguf` from the default `python`; `PYTHONPATH` is preset
49	  (`python -I` ignores it and will not find the module). `gguf-py` can parse
50	  this GGUF and expose the raw tensor bytes and metadata; it has no PTQ1_0
51	  dequantizer and no runtime tokenizer.
52	- **Data**: `data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0.gguf` (the model),
53	  `data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0-f16.safetensors` (dequantized weights),
54	  and `data/samples/` (sample prompts/corpus). `TOKENIZER-VECTORS.json` gives
55	  reference token ids for visible strings.
56	- **Reference**: `ref/bin/{llama-cli,llama-debug,llama-perplexity,bonsai-ref,bonsai-ref-cpu}`
57	  are stripped llama.cpp builds. `-ngl 0` / `-ngl 99` or `ctx ... cpu|vulkan`
58	  select the backend; `bonsai-ref-cpu` has no Vulkan backend. The Vulkan backend
59	  runs at roughly 130–180 token/s generation and 2,600–3,500 token/s prefill on
60	  this GPU; the CPU backend is memory-bandwidth-bound at roughly 10–35 token/s,
61	  so reserve it for tokenizer checks and short spot checks. `ref/PROTOCOL.md`
62	  describes the line protocol.
63	- **Reference use — black box.** Run the reference binaries through their
64	  documented CLI and line protocol only. Do **not** disassemble, decompile,
65	  debug, or otherwise analyze the binaries, and do not read them with `strings`,
66	  `nm`, `readelf`, `objdump`, `llvm-objdump`, `gdb`, `lldb`, custom ELF parsers
67	  or disassembler bindings; do not link to or reuse their code. Recover the
68	  architecture from the GGUF, the safetensors development copy and the
69	  documented runner output. Treating `ref/bin` as anything other than a
70	  black-box oracle is non-compliant.
71	- **Docs**: `docs/` contains the Vulkan 1.4 spec, Roadmap 2026 appendix and
72	  profile, SPIR-V/GLSL specs, GGUF spec, Vulkan Profiles overview, and Zig docs.
73	
74	## Bash command classification
75	
76	Claude Code may deny a safe Bash command when it is compound. Prefer one simple
77	command per call, do not set environment variables to paths outside the
78	workspace, and if a command is still denied, put it in a workspace script and
79	run the script.
80	
81	## Time budget
82	
83	The session is terminated at a fixed wall-clock deadline. `BENCH_DEADLINE_EPOCH`
84	holds the deadline as Unix time, and `time-left` prints the remaining time. The
85	default budget is 2 hours; trust the environment variable if it differs.
86	
87	Only files in this workspace at the deadline are graded. The conversation is
88	not saved for grading, so write code, run tests and update `NOTES.md`
89	continuously rather than leaving everything to the end. Plan the budget: the
90	Vulkan reference is fast enough for frequent checks, the CPU reference is slow,
91	and hidden grading uses precomputed CPU values, so CPU inference is never
92	required.
93	
94	## Target and constraints
95	
96	- Target **Vulkan 1.4** and the compute-relevant Vulkan Roadmap 2026 feature
97	  subset in `DEVICE.md`. The GPU does not support three non-compute Roadmap 2026
98	  items (presentation/copy/host-image); those are not required.
99	- The engine must create a Vulkan device from the provided GPU and run the
100	  model's forward pass on it. **Model computation** means every arithmetic
101	  operation on model weights or activations in the forward pass, including
102	  normalization, activations (silu/sigmoid), softmax, RoPE, the GDN
103	  recurrence, conv1d, KV-cache updates and projections. All of it must be
104	  issued as Vulkan compute work. CPU code is limited to tokenization, Vulkan
105	  command/memory orchestration and I/O; CPU tensor arithmetic is a violation,
106	  including a CPU fallback used when Vulkan initialization fails (fail
107	  instead). A submission that performs model computation on the CPU is
108	  non-compliant even if it passes correctness and the VRAM residency gate.
109	- Support at least `n_ctx = 16384`; the harness creates contexts up to 16384
110	  (the long greedy case and the VRAM measurement). The model's training context
111	  is 262144.
112	- The harness calls the ABI single-threaded; the engine may use its own worker
113	  threads. Calls must not crash on malformed input; return a negative error and
114	  set `bonsai_last_error()`.
115	- Model execution must be deterministic for a fixed token sequence (greedy,
116	  no sampling randomness).
117	
118	## Correctness and scoring
119	
120	Correctness is the primary acceptance criterion; it is measured against
121	precomputed CPU llama.cpp golden values, using the same methodology as the
122	reference CPU-vs-Vulkan comparison (tokenizer IDs, dequantized tensors, logits,
123	per-position agreement, greedy tokens). Grading does not run CPU inference.
124	Performance is the optimization target; VRAM is a secondary acceptance gate. The
125	exact metrics and reference thresholds are in `ACCEPTANCE.md`. Hidden tests use
126	prompts and corpora not present here.
127	
128	Do not modify `data/`, `docs/`, or `ref/`.
129	
130	When done, leave `NOTES.md` with your design, known limitations, and measured
131	results.

# Task: a Vulkan inference engine for Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B

Implement **`bonsai-vk`**, a Vulkan inference engine for the model in
`data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0.gguf`, written in **Zig 0.17.0** using
**Vulkan SDK 1.4.363.0**.

The engine must load the GGUF file at runtime, reproduce the model's logits and
greedy token sequence, and be as fast as possible on the provided AMD GPU.
`ref/` contains symbol-stripped llama.cpp binaries with CPU and Vulkan backends
and a reference runner; use them as the correctness oracle. `data/` also
contains the dequantized weights as a safetensors file for development.

## Deliverable

A Zig project at the root of this directory that builds offline with:

```
zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast
```

`ABI.md` (`extern "C"`, no C++ mangling, no extra required runtime files).

The library must be self-contained:

- It reads only the GGUF path passed by the harness. It must not read the
  safetensors file, a converted sidecar, or any other model file at runtime.
- It must not embed model weights or precomputed results in the submission.
- It must not link to or execute llama.cpp/ggml, or any prebuilt inference
  engine. All model computation must go through Vulkan compute shaders; the
  definition of model computation and the CPU allowlist are under Target and
  constraints.
- No network access is available. The build must not fetch dependencies.
- The grading build runs in a clean container containing only the files you
  submit. `data/`, `docs/` and `ref/` are not present at build time; do not
  read them from `build.zig` or embed them, and do not hard-code `/workspace`
  paths. Anything the build needs must live in the submission.

  this Zig version; `zig translate-c` is.

command per call, do not set environment variables to paths outside the

run the script.

holds the deadline as Unix time, and `time-left` prints the remaining time. The
default budget is 2 hours; trust the environment variable if it differs.

not saved for grading, so write code, run tests and update `NOTES.md`
continuously rather than leaving everything to the end. Plan the budget: the

required.

10	- `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast` succeeds offline in a clean container and
11	  produces `zig-out/lib/libbonsai.so`.
12	- The library exports the ABI in `ABI.md` and loads the GGUF path supplied by
13	  the harness.
14	- It does not read the safetensors file or any sidecar model file at runtime,
15	  does not embed model weights, does not link/execute llama.cpp or another
16	  inference engine, and does not use the network.
17	- All model computation uses Vulkan 1.4 with the compute subset of Roadmap 2026
18	  in `DEVICE.md`. "Model computation" is every arithmetic operation on model
19	  weights or activations in the forward pass (normalization, activations,
20	  softmax, RoPE, the GDN recurrence, conv1d, KV-cache updates, projections).
21	  CPU is limited to tokenization, Vulkan command/memory orchestration and I/O;
22	  CPU tensor arithmetic is a violation, including a CPU fallback.
23	- Correctness and the VRAM residency gate do not prove GPU computation: a CPU
24	  implementation with the weights resident in VRAM passes both. This is a
25	  structural requirement subject to source review; documented CPU model math
26	  makes the submission non-compliant.
27	- `ref/bin` is used only as a black box: running the documented CLI/protocol is
28	  allowed; disassembly, `strings`/`nm`/`readelf`/`objdump`, debugger use, ELF
29	  parsing or reusing the reference's code is non-compliant.
30	- No prebuilt engine binary; only source and build scripts are submitted.
31	- The grading build runs in a clean container containing only the submitted
32	  files. `data/`, `docs/` and `ref/` are not present during the build; do not
33	  read them at build time or hard-code `/workspace` paths.
34	
35	## 2. Correctness (primary)
36	
37	Hidden prompts and corpora are different from `data/samples/`. Golden values
38	are precomputed by the verifier with the CPU llama.cpp backend; grading does
39	not run CPU inference. The correctness score is a weighted mean:
40	
41	| suite | weight | metric |
42	|---|---:|---|
43	| tokenizer | 0.10 | fraction of hidden strings whose token ids match exactly |
44	| dequant | 0.15 | fraction of sampled tensors whose f32 values match the reference exactly (PTQ1_0 dequantized values widened to f32; F32 copied) and whose `tensor_info` type/rank/shape match the GGUF |
45	| logits | 0.30 | per prompt at n_ctx 512/2048/4096/8192: top-1 match, mean KL, cosine |
46	| positions | 0.15 | hidden corpus at n_ctx 512/2048: top-1 agreement and mean KL across positions |
47	| greedy | 0.30 | teacher-forced agreement over 64 steps after 64/2048/8192-token prompts (n_ctx 1024/4096/16384), plus a `generate` smoke test |
48	
49	Reference points from the CPU-vs-Vulkan llama.cpp comparison on this machine:
50	logits cosine 0.9998–0.99997, top-1 agreement 97.8–98.8%, mean KLD
51	0.0007–0.0008 nats. Greedy steps are compared teacher-forced (free-running
52	sequences diverge after the first flipped token, so sequence equality is not a
53	useful metric at long context).
54	
55	Reference (full-credit) operating points:
56	
57	- tokenizer and dequant: exact;
58	- top-1 agreement ≥ 95%;
59	- mean KL ≤ 0.01 nats;
60	- cosine similarity ≥ 0.995;
61	- teacher-forced greedy agreement ≥ 95% (and `generate` must pass its smoke
62	  test).
63	
64	The verifier converts each component into a [0,1] score and reports the suite
65	breakdown. **Acceptance requires a correctness score ≥ 0.90.** The CPU-vs-Vulkan
66	llama.cpp reference scores about 0.99 under this formula. The verifier is
67	authoritative.
68	
69	## 3. Performance (optimization target)
70	
71	Measured only after correctness acceptance:
72	
73	- pp (prompt processing): 512/2048/4096/8192-token prompts in one eval.
74	- tg (generation): 128 greedy tokens after context depths 0/512/2048/4096/8192.
75	- Reference: the stripped llama.cpp **Vulkan** binary on the same GPU, same
76	  contexts, same greedy policy, same machine.
77	- Score: geometric mean of `agent tokens/s / reference tokens/s` across the
78	  pp and tg tests. pp and tg results are reported separately.
79	- Warmup, repeated runs, and medians are used. Performance is only scored when
80	  the correctness suites pass; the perf prompts come from the hidden corpus, so
81	  they cannot be special-cased.
82	
83	## 4. VRAM (secondary acceptance gate)
84	
85	The harness polls peak process VRAM from `drm-memory-vram` in
86	`/proc/<pid>/fdinfo` (deduplicated by DRM client id) across the whole run,
87	including the largest context (n_ctx 16384), and reads peak host RSS from
88	`VmHWM`. The reference (llama.cpp Vulkan) is measured with the same workload,
89	sampling during decode.
90	
91	- Peak VRAM must satisfy
92	  `peak ≤ max(1.5 × reference_peak, reference_peak + 512 MiB)`.
93	- Peak host RSS must satisfy `peak ≤ reference_RSS + 2 GiB`.
94	- Peak VRAM must be at least ~450 MiB (half the packed model size) to
95	  demonstrate that the model is resident on the GPU rather than computed on
96	  the CPU.
97	
98	The gate is sized so that a pre-dequantized copy of the weights cannot pass;
99	the packed model must stay resident. Failing the VRAM gate sets the performance
100	score to zero; correctness is still reported. The reference peak/RSS are
101	measured by the verifier on the same GPU.
102	
103	## 5. Anti-cheat and hygiene
104	
105	- The engine must derive all weights from the GGUF at the supplied path. A
106	  submission that embeds weights, reads a generated sidecar, or depends on the
107	  safetensors file is rejected.
108	- The reference binaries are not present in the grading container; the engine
109	  may not spawn them or link llama.cpp/ggml.
110	- The submission source must be under 32 MiB (excluding `data/`, `docs/`,
111	  `ref/`, Zig build outputs, temporary files and Claude Code state); embedding
112	  model weights, a foreign engine binary or generated data is rejected. Linked
113	  libraries are checked. No network is available.
114	- The ABI permits worker threads, not child processes. The harness records
115	  `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` and live children of the grading process; a library that
116	  spawns a helper process (for example an embedded engine binary) scores zero.
117	- The engine must be deterministic for a fixed token sequence.
118	- Do not modify `data/`, `docs/`, or `ref/`.
119	
120	## 6. Deliverable notes
121	
122	The session is terminated at the deadline in `BENCH_DEADLINE_EPOCH`; only
123	workspace files present at that moment are graded. Save code and notes
124	continuously.
125	
126	Leave `NOTES.md` with:
127	
128	- the engine design and which Vulkan features it uses,
129	- known limitations and unsupported cases,
130	- measured correctness and pp/tg results,
131	- peak VRAM at the contexts you tested.

typedef struct bonsai_context bonsai_context;

int32_t  bonsai_n_ctx_train(const bonsai_model *model);

int32_t  bonsai_tensor_info(const bonsai_model *model, int32_t index,

                               int32_t n_batch, bonsai_context **out_ctx);

  harness.

  `context_length` metadata.

- If `ids != NULL` and `capacity < required`, return `BONSAI_ERR_CAPACITY`.

# Target GPU and Vulkan feature set

The benchmark runs on one machine:

- GPU: **AMD Radeon RX 9070** (RDNA4, `RADV GFX1201`), 16304 MiB VRAM
- Driver: Mesa 26.0.8 (RADV), device `apiVersion` **1.4.335**
- Loader: Vulkan SDK **1.4.363.0**
- The driver prints `radv is not a conformant Vulkan implementation, testing use only.`
  This is expected; it is the target device.

The engine must target **Vulkan 1.4** and the compute-relevant subset of
**Vulkan Roadmap 2026**. The full profile is not implementable on this GPU; the
three missing items are presentation/copy/host-image features that a headless
inference engine does not need.

## Full VP_KHR_roadmap_2026 gaps (not required)

| missing item | kind |
|---|---|
| `VK_KHR_copy_memory_indirect` + `indirectMemoryCopy` | device extension/feature |
| `VK_KHR_present_mode_fifo_latest_ready` + `presentModeFifoLatestReady` | device extension/feature |
| `hostImageCopy` | Vulkan 1.4 core feature |

The line-rasterization requirement is an OR-group; the device satisfies it via
rectangular/Bresenham/smooth/stippled-Bresenham. The required 2026 limits are
all met.

## Required compute feature set (all supported)

Core Vulkan 1.4 features, including:

- `shaderFloat16`, `shaderInt8`
- `storageBuffer16BitAccess`, `storageBuffer8BitAccess`
- `shaderIntegerDotProduct` (8-bit paths accelerated)
- `timelineSemaphore`, `bufferDeviceAddress`, `descriptorIndexing`
- `scalarBlockLayout`, `vulkanMemoryModel`

Extensions/features:

- `VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix` (revision 2; compute stage;
  `cooperativeMatrix = true`)
- `VK_KHR_maintenance5`, `VK_KHR_maintenance7`, `VK_KHR_maintenance8`,
  `VK_KHR_maintenance9`
- `VK_KHR_shader_float_controls2`
- `VK_KHR_shader_expect_assume`
- `VK_KHR_shader_subgroup_rotate`
- `VK_KHR_shader_subgroup_uniform_control_flow`
- `VK_KHR_shader_maximal_reconvergence`
- `VK_KHR_shader_quad_control`
- `VK_KHR_shader_untyped_pointers`
- `VK_KHR_workgroup_memory_explicit_layout`
- `VK_KHR_robustness2` (`robustBufferAccess2`, `robustImageAccess2`,
  `nullDescriptor`)
- `VK_KHR_pipeline_binary`, `VK_KHR_map_memory2`
- `VK_KHR_shader_clock`, `VK_KHR_compute_shader_derivatives`

The device reports `matrix cores: KHR_coopmat`, `int dot: 1`, `fp16: 1`,
`bf16: 1`. Cooperative matrix is supported in compute shaders; `glslc` from the
SDK compiles `GL_KHR_cooperative_matrix` f16/f32 SPIR-V.

## Querying the device

`vulkaninfo` is on `PATH`. The benchmark image also provides a captured
`docs/device/vulkaninfo.json` (`vulkaninfo -j`), the Roadmap 2026 profile
(`docs/device/VP_KHR_roadmap.json`), and the roadmap appendix
(`docs/device/Roadmap-2026.adoc`).

Suggested checks:

```bash
vulkaninfo --summary
vulkaninfo | grep -i -A20 "VkPhysicalDeviceVulkan14Features"
glslc --version
spirv-val --target-env vulkan1.4 shader.spv
```

## Practical notes

- Use the SDK loader:
  `-I "$VULKAN_SDK/include" -L "$VULKAN_SDK/lib/VulkanLoader/lib" -lvulkan`,
  and run with `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` including that directory.
- The SDK is at `$VULKAN_SDK` (`/opt/vulkan-sdk` in the benchmark image).
- Use `VK_ICD_FILENAMES=/usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/radeon_icd.json` if automatic
  ICD discovery is a problem.
- Validation layers are installed; `VK_INSTANCE_LAYERS=VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation`
  is useful while developing, but disable them for performance measurements.
- `vkprofiles` can inspect the profile file; the exact compute feature list
  above is the authoritative scope for this benchmark.

1	# C ABI contract
2	
3	The grader loads `zig-out/lib/libbonsai.so` with `dlopen` and drives it through
4	the C ABI below. The canonical header is `examples/abi/bonsai.h`; this document
5	defines the semantics the harness relies on.
6	
7	```c
8	typedef struct bonsai_model   bonsai_model;
9	typedef struct bonsai_context bonsai_context;
10	
11	uint32_t    bonsai_abi_version(void);       /* returns 1 */
12	const char *bonsai_last_error(void);        /* thread-local; NULL if none */
13	
14	int32_t  bonsai_model_open(const char *gguf_path, bonsai_model **out_model);
15	void     bonsai_model_close(bonsai_model *model);
16	int32_t  bonsai_n_vocab(const bonsai_model *model);
17	int32_t  bonsai_n_ctx_train(const bonsai_model *model);
18	
19	int32_t  bonsai_tokenize(const bonsai_model *model, const char *utf8,
20	                         int32_t add_bos, int32_t *ids, int32_t capacity);
21	
22	int32_t  bonsai_tensor_count(const bonsai_model *model);
23	int32_t  bonsai_tensor_info(const bonsai_model *model, int32_t index,
24	                            const char **name, int32_t *ggml_type,
25	                            int32_t *rank, int64_t ne[4]);
26	int64_t  bonsai_tensor_dequant(const bonsai_model *model, const char *name,
27	                               float *out, int64_t capacity);
28	
29	int32_t  bonsai_context_create(bonsai_model *model, int32_t n_ctx,
30	                               int32_t n_batch, bonsai_context **out_ctx);
31	void     bonsai_context_close(bonsai_context *ctx);
32	int32_t  bonsai_context_reset(bonsai_context *ctx);
33	int32_t  bonsai_eval(bonsai_context *ctx, const int32_t *tokens, int32_t n_tokens,
34	                     float *logits, int32_t logits_capacity);
35	int32_t  bonsai_generate_greedy(bonsai_context *ctx,
36	                                const int32_t *prompt, int32_t n_prompt,
37	                                int32_t n_predict, uint32_t flags,
38	                                int32_t *out_ids);
39	```
40	
41	## Build artifact
42	
43	- `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast` at the submission root must produce
44	  `zig-out/lib/libbonsai.so`.
45	- Symbols are C linkage (`extern "C"`), no C++ mangling, no extra shared
46	  libraries except the system Vulkan loader/libc. The grader checks that the
47	  library does not link llama.cpp/ggml.
48	- The library must be safe to `dlopen` without environment variables or files
49	  beside the GGUF path.
50	
51	## Model
52	
53	- `bonsai_model_open` parses the GGUF at `gguf_path`. It must not open any other
54	  model/weight file. The path is a normal filesystem path supplied by the
55	  harness.
56	- `bonsai_n_vocab` returns the vocabulary size from the GGUF tokenizer
57	  metadata.
58	- `bonsai_n_ctx_train` returns the model context length from the GGUF
59	  `context_length` metadata.
60	- Multiple models may be opened, but the tests normally use one.
61	- Errors: return a negative code and set a human-readable `bonsai_last_error`.
62	
63	## Tokenizer
64	
65	- `bonsai_tokenize` implements the model's tokenizer from the GGUF metadata:
66	  GPT-2 byte-level BPE with the `qwen35` pre-tokenizer described in
67	  `TOKENIZER.md`.
68	- `add_bos != 0` requests BOS insertion. This model's GGUF sets
69	  `tokenizer.ggml.add_bos_token = false`, so the reference (`llama_tokenize`
70	  with `add_special = add_bos != 0`) does **not** prepend BOS even when
71	  `add_bos != 0`; the ids are the same as with `add_bos = 0`. The harness
72	  always calls with `add_bos = 0`.
73	- Special tokens contained in the GGUF vocabulary are matched atomically as
74	  their UTF-8 byte sequences. No chat template is applied.
75	- If `ids == NULL`, return the required number of ids without writing.
76	- If `ids != NULL` and `capacity < required`, return `BONSAI_ERR_CAPACITY`.
77	- The token stream must exactly match llama.cpp's tokenizer for the same flags.
78	
79	## Tensor introspection (staged tests)
80	
81	- `bonsai_tensor_count` returns the number of tensors in the GGUF.
82	- `bonsai_tensor_info` returns the tensor name (owned by the model), the numeric
83	  GGML type id (as reported by `gguf-py`), the rank, and `ne[0..3]` in **GGUF
84	  order** (`ne[0]` is the contiguous/inner dimension).
85	- `bonsai_tensor_dequant` writes the tensor to `out` as **f32** in PyTorch /
86	  safetensors row-major order: the GGUF dimensions are reversed, so `ne[0]`
87	  varies fastest and element `(i1, i0)` is at `i1*ne[0] + i0`.
88	- For PTQ1_0 the values must match the reference dequantization bit-exactly
89	  (no approximation tolerance is applied). For F32 tensors the values are
90	  copied bit-exactly.
91	- Returns the element count, or `BONSAI_ERR_CAPACITY` if `capacity` is too
92	  small.
93	
94	## Context and evaluation
95	
96	- `bonsai_context_create` allocates a context with `n_ctx` positions. `n_batch`
97	  is a processing hint; the engine may choose its own internal batching.
98	- `bonsai_context_reset` discards all KV/recurrent state and positions.
99	- `bonsai_eval` appends `n_tokens` token ids (n_tokens >= 1) and evaluates
100	  them. The token ids are already tokenized; the engine must not re-tokenize
101	  them.
102	- If `logits != NULL`, it must point to at least `n_vocab` floats; the engine
103	  writes the f32 logits for the **last token**. If `capacity < n_vocab`,
104	  return `BONSAI_ERR_CAPACITY`.
105	- The engine must support incremental calls: `bonsai_eval` on a prompt followed
106	  by repeated `bonsai_eval` with one token, producing the same state as one
107	  large call.
108	- Position indices advance by the number of tokens appended; reset starts at 0.
109	
110	## Greedy generation
111	
112	- `bonsai_generate_greedy` evaluates `prompt[0..n_prompt)` (may be empty), then
113	  selects the argmax token of the last-token logits, appends it, and repeats up
114	  to `n_predict` times.
115	- It writes generated token ids to `out_ids` (capacity at least `n_predict`) and
116	  returns the count. It stops early at the model's EOS token (from the GGUF
117	  tokenizer metadata) unless
118	  `BONSAI_GEN_IGNORE_EOS` is set.
119	- Determinism is required: same prompt and context size produce the same ids.
120	- After the call the context state is unspecified; the harness resets it.
121	
122	## Errors and robustness
123	
124	- `bonsai_last_error` returns a thread-local NUL-terminated string, valid until
125	  the next API call on that thread, or NULL.
126	- The library must not call `exit`, abort, or install signal handlers. Invalid
127	  arguments and allocation failures return negative codes.
128	- All API calls are made from one thread at a time. The engine may spawn worker
129	  threads internally; it must join/free them in `close`.
130

# Model: Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B (`qwen35`)

The model is `data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0.gguf`. Its GGUF metadata and
tensor inventory are the source of truth for dimensions, tensor names, shapes
and quantization types; parse them with the provided `gguf-py` reader or
directly.

**This document intentionally does not describe the architecture.** The layer
structure, tensor ordering, weight representation and numerical behavior are
part of the task. Recover them from the GGUF, the dequantized development
tensors in `data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0-f16.safetensors` (development only;
never read at runtime), and the reference runner.

`ref/bin/bonsai-ref` is the numerical oracle; `ref/PROTOCOL.md` documents its
line protocol. Where your interpretation disagrees with the oracle, the oracle
wins.

Contract notes:

- The engine loads the GGUF at runtime and derives every weight from it; it must
  not read the safetensors file, embed weights, or use another engine.
- `bonsai_tensor_dequant` must match the reference dequantization exactly.
  Logits, per-position agreement and greedy tokens are scored against the CPU
  oracle (`ABI.md`, `ACCEPTANCE.md`).
- The ABI and context semantics are in `ABI.md`; the tokenizer is specified in
  `TOKENIZER.md`.

1	# Tokenizer specification
2	
3	The GGUF contains the complete tokenizer dictionary and configuration:
4	
5	| key | value |
6	|---|---|
7	| `tokenizer.ggml.model` | `gpt2` |
8	| `tokenizer.ggml.pre` | `qwen35` |
9	| `tokenizer.ggml.tokens` | 248,320 strings |
10	| `tokenizer.ggml.merges` | 247,587 merge rules |
11	| `tokenizer.ggml.token_type` | 248,320 type codes |
12	| `tokenizer.ggml.bos_token_id` | 248044 |
13	| `tokenizer.ggml.eos_token_id` | 248046 |
14	| `tokenizer.ggml.padding_token_id` | 248044 |
15	| `tokenizer.ggml.add_bos_token` | false |
16	| `tokenizer.chat_template` | Jinja template (not used by the ABI) |
17	
18	This is a **GPT-2 byte-level BPE** tokenizer, not SentencePiece. The dictionary
19	and merges come from the GGUF; the missing details are the byte mapping and the
20	`qwen35` pre-tokenization rule.
21	
22	## 1. Byte-to-unicode mapping
23	
24	Map each raw byte to a printable Unicode code point (the standard GPT-2 table):
25	
26	```python
27	bs = list(range(ord("!"), ord("~") + 1)) + \
28	     list(range(ord("¡"), ord("¬") + 1)) + \
29	     list(range(ord("®"), ord("ÿ") + 1))
30	cs = bs[:]
31	n = 0
32	for b in range(256):
33	    if b not in bs:
34	        bs.append(b)
35	        cs.append(256 + n)
36	        n += 1
37	byte_to_unicode = {b: chr(c) for b, c in zip(bs, cs)}
38	```
39	
40	Tokens in the GGUF are already strings in this representation (for example a
41	leading space is `Ġ`). Merges are two such strings separated by a space.
42	
43	## 2. Pre-tokenization (`qwen35`)
44	
45	Before BPE, split the UTF-8-decoded text with this regex (equivalent to the
46	case-insensitive original used by the tokenizer):
47	
48	```
49	(?:'[sS]|'[tT]|'[rR][eE]|'[vV][eE]|'[mM]|'[lL][lL]|'[dD])
50	|[^\r\n\p{L}\p{N}]?[\p{L}\p{M}]+
51	|\p{N}
52	| ?[^\s\p{L}\p{M}\p{N}]+[\r\n]*
53	|\s*[\r\n]+
54	|\s+(?!\S)
55	|\s+
56	```
57	
58	This is the `qwen35` rule: letters may include combining marks (`\p{M}`),
59	unlike the older Qwen2 rule. `clean_spaces = false`: do not strip leading
60	spaces from the pre-tokenized pieces.
61	
62	## 3. BPE merges
63	
64	For each pre-token:
65	
66	1. Convert its raw UTF-8 bytes to the byte-to-unicode string.
67	2. Split into individual symbols.
68	3. Repeatedly merge the adjacent pair whose concatenation has the **lowest
69	   index** in `tokenizer.ggml.merges` (the list order is the merge rank), until
70	   no pair is present. Ties are resolved by the leftmost occurrence.
71	4. Map each resulting symbol to its index in `tokenizer.ggml.tokens`; that index
72	   is the token id.
73	
74	The merges are the usual `"left right"` strings, e.g. `Ġ Ġ` or `i n`. There are
75	247,587 entries; token id 0 is the first entry of the tokens array.
76	
77	## 4. Special tokens and BOS
78	
79	- Tokens whose type marks them as control/user-defined/special are matched
80	  **atomically** in the input text before BPE (e.g. `<|im_start|>`); they are
81	  emitted as their exact token ids.
82	- `add_bos_token` is false in the GGUF. The reference passes
83	  `add_special = (add_bos != 0)` to llama.cpp, which honors this metadata, so
84	  `add_bos` does **not** prepend BOS for this model; `ids_add_bos` in
85	  `TOKENIZER-VECTORS.json` is therefore identical to `ids`. The harness uses
86	  `add_bos = 0`.
87	- EOS is 248046; padding is 248044.
88	- The ABI does not apply the chat template. The harness tokenizes raw text and
89	  compares token ids with the reference tokenizer.
90	
91	## 5. Validation
92	
93	`ref/bin/bonsai-ref` and `llama-cli` use the same tokenizer; use them to obtain
94	reference ids for arbitrary strings. `TOKENIZER-VECTORS.json` in this directory
95	lists reference ids for 15 visible strings (`ids_add_bos` is shown for
96	completeness and is identical to `ids` for this model). `data/samples/`
97	contains a few visible sample texts; hidden tests use different strings,
98	including Unicode, combining marks, code, whitespace and special tokens.
99	
100	The tokenizer is part of the correctness score (exact token ids). The dequant,
101	forward-pass and generation suites use token ids supplied by the harness, so a
102	tokenizer bug does not hide an inference bug.
103

# Tokenizer specification

The GGUF contains the complete tokenizer dictionary and configuration:

| key | value |
|---|---|
| `tokenizer.ggml.model` | `gpt2` |
| `tokenizer.ggml.pre` | `qwen35` |
| `tokenizer.ggml.tokens` | 248,320 strings |
| `tokenizer.ggml.merges` | 247,587 merge rules |
| `tokenizer.ggml.token_type` | 248,320 type codes |
| `tokenizer.ggml.bos_token_id` | 248044 |
| `tokenizer.ggml.eos_token_id` | 248046 |
| `tokenizer.ggml.padding_token_id` | 248044 |
| `tokenizer.ggml.add_bos_token` | false |
| `tokenizer.chat_template` | Jinja template (not used by the ABI) |

This is a **GPT-2 byte-level BPE** tokenizer, not SentencePiece. The dictionary
and merges come from the GGUF; the missing details are the byte mapping and the
`qwen35` pre-tokenization rule.

## 1. Byte-to-unicode mapping

Map each raw byte to a printable Unicode code point (the standard GPT-2 table):

```python
bs = list(range(ord("!"), ord("~") + 1)) + \
     list(range(ord("¡"), ord("¬") + 1)) + \
     list(range(ord("®"), ord("ÿ") + 1))
cs = bs[:]
n = 0
for b in range(256):
    if b not in bs:
        bs.append(b)
        cs.append(256 + n)
        n += 1

```

Tokens in the GGUF are already strings in this representation (for example a
leading space is `Ġ`). Merges are two such strings separated by a space.

## 2. Pre-tokenization (`qwen35`)

Before BPE, split the UTF-8-decoded text with this regex (equivalent to the
case-insensitive original used by the tokenizer):

```
(?:'[sS]|'[tT]|'[rR][eE]|'[vV][eE]|'[mM]|'[lL][lL]|'[dD])
|[^\r\n\p{L}\p{N}]?[\p{L}\p{M}]+
|\p{N}
| ?[^\s\p{L}\p{M}\p{N}]+[\r\n]*
|\s*[\r\n]+
|\s+(?!\S)
|\s+
```

This is the `qwen35` rule: letters may include combining marks (`\p{M}`),
unlike the older Qwen2 rule. `clean_spaces = false`: do not strip leading
spaces from the pre-tokenized pieces.

## 3. BPE merges

For each pre-token:

1. Convert its raw UTF-8 bytes to the byte-to-unicode string.
2. Split into individual symbols.
3. Repeatedly merge the adjacent pair whose concatenation has the **lowest
   index** in `tokenizer.ggml.merges` (the list order is the merge rank), until
   no pair is present. Ties are resolved by the leftmost occurrence.
4. Map each resulting symbol to its index in `tokenizer.ggml.tokens`; that index
   is the token id.

The merges are the usual `"left right"` strings, e.g. `Ġ Ġ` or `i n`. There are
247,587 entries; token id 0 is the first entry of the tokens array.

## 4. Special tokens and BOS

- Tokens whose type marks them as control/user-defined/special are matched
  **atomically** in the input text before BPE (e.g. `<|im_start|>`); they are
  emitted as their exact token ids.

  `TOKENIZER-VECTORS.json` is therefore identical to `ids`. The harness uses
  `add_bos = 0`.
- EOS is 248046; padding is 248044.
- The ABI does not apply the chat template. The harness tokenizes raw text and
  compares token ids with the reference tokenizer.

## 5. Validation

`ref/bin/bonsai-ref` and `llama-cli` use the same tokenizer; use them to obtain
reference ids for arbitrary strings. `TOKENIZER-VECTORS.json` in this directory

completeness and is identical to `ids` for this model). `data/samples/`
contains a few visible sample texts; hidden tests use different strings,
including Unicode, combining marks, code, whitespace and special tokens.

The tokenizer is part of the correctness score (exact token ids). The dequant,
forward-pass and generation suites use token ids supplied by the harness, so a
tokenizer bug does not hide an inference bug.

1	# Reference runner protocol
2	
3	`ref/bin/bonsai-ref` is a symbol-stripped llama.cpp runner (CPU and Vulkan
4	backends) for the benchmark model. It reads one command per line on stdin and
5	replies with exactly one line on stdout.
6	
7	```
8	load <model.gguf>
9	info
10	tokenize <hex-utf8> [add_bos]
11	ctx <id> <n_ctx> <cpu|vulkan>
12	reset <id>
13	eval <id> <n_tokens> <token_id>...
14	logits <id> <output.bin>
15	gen <id> <n_predict> [ignore_eos]
16	quit
17	```
18	
19	| command | reply |
20	|---|---|
21	| `load <path>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
22	| `info` | `ok arch=<arch> n_layer=<n> n_embd=<n> n_vocab=<n> n_ctx_train=<n>` |
23	| `tokenize <hex> [1]` | `ok <n> <id>...` / `error <msg>` |
24	| `ctx <id> <n_ctx> <cpu\|vulkan>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
25	| `reset <id>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
26	| `eval <id> <n> <id>...` | `ok` / `error <msg>` (appends and evaluates) |
27	| `logits <id> <path>` | `ok <n_vocab>`; writes raw little-endian f32 logits for the last token |
28	| `gen <id> <n> [1]` | `ok <n_generated> <id>...` (greedy; stops at EOS unless the last argument is `1`) |
29	| `quit` | exits |
30	
31	Notes:
32	
33	- `<hex-utf8>` is the lowercase hex encoding of the UTF-8 text. This avoids
34	  quoting issues. Example: `tokenize 48656c6c6f` for `Hello`.
35	- `tokenize` uses the model's `qwen35` tokenizer; `add_bos` defaults to 0.
36	- `ctx` creates a context with `n_ctx` positions. `cpu` uses `-ngl 0`;
37	  `vulkan` uses the Vulkan backend with all layers offloaded.
38	- `eval` token ids are appended to the context in order; the context must have
39	  room. Call `reset` between independent prompts.
40	- `logits` writes `n_vocab` float32 values in model-vocabulary order.
41	- `gen` selects argmax at each step and appends the token; no sampling
42	  parameters.
43	- All state is deterministic for a fixed sequence.
44	- The CPU backend is memory-bandwidth-bound on this machine: expect tens of
45	  tokens/s, versus hundreds on the Vulkan backend (and thousands for prefill).
46	  Use `cpu` for tokenizer, metadata and short spot checks; use `vulkan` for
47	  iteration. The grader compares against precomputed CPU golden values, so you
48	  do not need to run CPU inference to be graded.
49	- `ref/bin/bonsai-ref-cpu` is the same runner built without the Vulkan backend;
50	  it accepts only `cpu` contexts and is useful for pure-CPU checks.
51	
52	`llama-cli`, `llama-debug` and `llama-perplexity` are also provided for
53	ad-hoc reference runs; `llama-cli -ngl 0` uses the CPU backend and
54	`llama-cli -ngl 99` the Vulkan backend.

content.content:
1	# Reference runner protocol
2	
3	`ref/bin/bonsai-ref` is a symbol-stripped llama.cpp runner (CPU and Vulkan
4	backends) for the benchmark model. It reads one command per line on stdin and
5	replies with exactly one line on stdout.
6	
7	```
8	load <model.gguf>
9	info
10	tokenize <hex-utf8> [add_bos]
11	ctx <id> <n_ctx> <cpu|vulkan>
12	reset <id>
13	eval <id> <n_tokens> <token_id>...
14	logits <id> <output.bin>
15	gen <id> <n_predict> [ignore_eos]
16	quit
17	```
18	
19	| command | reply |
20	|---|---|
21	| `load <path>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
22	| `info` | `ok arch=<arch> n_layer=<n> n_embd=<n> n_vocab=<n> n_ctx_train=<n>` |
23	| `tokenize <hex> [1]` | `ok <n> <id>...` / `error <msg>` |
24	| `ctx <id> <n_ctx> <cpu\|vulkan>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
25	| `reset <id>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
26	| `eval <id> <n> <id>...` | `ok` / `error <msg>` (appends and evaluates) |
27	| `logits <id> <path>` | `ok <n_vocab>`; writes raw little-endian f32 logits for the last token |
28	| `gen <id> <n> [1]` | `ok <n_generated> <id>...` (greedy; stops at EOS unless the last argument is `1`) |
29	| `quit` | exits |
30	
31	Notes:
32	
33	- `<hex-utf8>` is the lowercase hex encoding of the UTF-8 text. This avoids
34	  quoting issues. Example: `tokenize 48656c6c6f` for `Hello`.
35	- `tokenize` uses the model's `qwen35` tokenizer; `add_bos` defaults to 0.
36	- `ctx` creates a context with `n_ctx` positions. `cpu` uses `-ngl 0`;
37	  `vulkan` uses the Vulkan backend with all layers offloaded.
38	- `eval` token ids are appended to the context in order; the context must have
39	  room. Call `reset` between independent prompts.
40	- `logits` writes `n_vocab` float32 values in model-vocabulary order.
41	- `gen` selects argmax at each step and appends the token; no sampling
42	  parameters.
43	- All state is deterministic for a fixed sequence.
44	- The CPU backend is memory-bandwidth-bound on this machine: expect tens of
45	  tokens/s, versus hundreds on the Vulkan backend (and thousands for prefill).
46	  Use `cpu` for tokenizer, metadata and short spot checks; use `vulkan` for
47	  iteration. The grader compares against precomputed CPU golden values, so you
48	  do not need to run CPU inference to be graded.
49	- `ref/bin/bonsai-ref-cpu` is the same runner built without the Vulkan backend;
50	  it accepts only `cpu` contexts and is useful for pure-CPU checks.
51	
52	`llama-cli`, `llama-debug` and `llama-perplexity` are also provided for
53	ad-hoc reference runs; `llama-cli -ngl 0` uses the CPU backend and
54	`llama-cli -ngl 99` the Vulkan backend.
55

import numpy as np, struct
from safetensors import safe_open
import gguf

r = gguf.GGUFReader("data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0.gguf")
t = [x for x in r.tensors if x.name == "blk.0.attn_gate.weight"][0]
raw = np.asarray(t.data).tobytes()
f = safe_open("data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0-f16.safetensors", framework="np")
arr = f.get_tensor("blk.0.attn_gate.weight").astype(np.float32).reshape(-1)

NB = 3000
q = np.zeros(NB*128, np.int8)
scales = np.zeros(NB, np.float32)
firsts = np.zeros(NB, np.float32)
bad = 0
for blk in range(NB):
    seg = arr[blk*128:(blk+1)*128]
    s = struct.unpack('<e', raw[blk*28+26:blk*28+28])[0]
    scales[blk] = s
    firsts[blk] = struct.unpack('<e', raw[blk*28:blk*28+2])[0]
    nz = np.isclose(seg, s, rtol=0, atol=0)
    nzneg = np.isclose(seg, -s, rtol=0, atol=0)
    zz = (seg == 0)
    if np.sum(nz)+np.sum(nzneg)+np.sum(zz) != 128:
        bad += 1
        if bad < 3:
            print("bad block", blk, np.unique(seg)[:8], s)
    q[blk*128:(blk+1)*128] = nz.astype(np.int8) - nzneg.astype(np.int8)
print("bad", bad)
print("sum per block unique:", np.unique(np.add.reduceat(q.astype(np.int32), np.arange(0,NB*128,128)))[:20])
print("zeros per block min/max:", np.min(np.sum(q.reshape(NB,128)==0,axis=1)), np.max(np.sum(q.reshape(NB,128)==0,axis=1)))
print("firsts stats", np.min(firsts), np.max(firsts), np.mean(np.abs(firsts)))
print("scales stats", np.min(scales), np.max(scales))
print("corr first/scale", np.corrcoef(np.abs(firsts), np.abs(scales))[0,1])
print("sample firsts", firsts[:10])
print("sample scales", scales[:10])
# relation between first f16 raw bits and the first values?
b0 = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.uint8).reshape(-1,28)[:NB]
print("byte hist per position:")
for i in range(28):
    print(i, np.min(b0[:,i]), np.max(b0[:,i]), np.mean(b0[:,i]))

import numpy as np
import gguf

r = gguf.GGUFReader("data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0.gguf")
names = ["token_embd.weight", "blk.0.attn_qkv.weight", "blk.3.attn_q.weight"]
for nm in names:
    t = [x for x in r.tensors if x.name == nm][0]
    a = np.asarray(t.data).tobytes()
    b = np.frombuffer(a, dtype=np.uint8)
    n = len(b)//28
    b = b[:n*28].reshape(n,28)
    print(nm, "blocks", n)
    for pos in [0,1,2,22,23,24,25,26,27]:
        col = b[:,pos]
        u = np.unique(col)
        missing = sorted(set(range(256)) - set(u.tolist()))
        print(" pos",pos,"min",col.min(),"max",col.max(),"mean",col.mean(),"nuniq",len(u),"missing_sample",missing[:12], "missing_count", len(missing))
    v16 = b[:,24].astype(np.uint32) | (b[:,25].astype(np.uint32)<<8)
    print(" u16@24 max", v16.max(), "min", v16.min(), "mean", v16.mean())
    v2 = b[:,0].astype(np.uint32) | (b[:,1].astype(np.uint32)<<8)
    print(" u16@0 max", v2.max(), "min", v2.min(), "mean", v2.mean())
    f16 = np.frombuffer(b[:,26:28].copy().tobytes(), dtype=np.float16)
    print(" f16@26 min/max", np.nanmin(f16), np.nanmax(f16), "nan", np.sum(np.isnan(f16)))

"""Numpy reference implementation of the bonsai qwen35 forward pass (dev only)."""
import numpy as np, struct, sys, json
from safetensors import safe_open

ST = "data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0-f16.safetensors"

class Cfg:
    n_layer=32; n_embd=2560; n_ff=9216; n_head=16; n_head_kv=4; head_dim=256
    rope_dim=64; rope_theta=1e7; eps=1e-6; n_vocab=248320
    conv_k=4; ssm_state=128; n_k_heads=16; n_v_heads=32; inner=4096
    full_attn_interval=4

class Model:
    def __init__(self, opts):
        self.o = opts
        self.f = safe_open(ST, framework="np")
        self.cache = {}
        self.cfg = Cfg()
        self.sign_widths = [2560,4096,9216]
        # sign vectors from GGUF metadata
        import gguf
        r = gguf.GGUFReader("data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0.gguf")
        f = r.fields

    def forward(self, toks, st):

        for il in range(self.cfg.n_layer):

                x = self.gdn(x, il, st[il])
            else:
                x = self.full_attn(x, il, st[il])
            x = self.ffn(x, il)
        return x


def main():
    opts = dict(sign_first=True, decay_first=False, q_layout='per_head')
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:

    m = Model(opts)
    toks = [int(x) for x in sys.argv[2].split(',')] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else [9419]
    out = sys.argv[3] if len(sys.argv) > 3 else "tools/nref_logits.bin"

    x = m.forward(toks, st)
    lg = m.logits(x[-1:])[0]
    lg.astype(np.float32).tofile(out)
    top = np.argsort(lg)[-10:][::-1]
    print("opts", opts, "toks", toks)
    print("top10", top.tolist(), lg[top].tolist())

    def ffn(self, x, il):
        h = self.rmsnorm(x, f"blk.{il}.post_attention_norm.weight")
        hf = self.tf(h)
        g = hf @ self.w(f"blk.{il}.ffn_gate.weight").T
        u = hf @ self.w(f"blk.{il}.ffn_up.weight").T
        a = (g/(1.0+np.exp(-g))) * u
        y = self.tf(a) @ self.w(f"blk.{il}.ffn_down.weight").T
        return x + y

    def new_state(self, n_ctx):
        c = self.cfg
        st = []
        for il in range(c.n_layer):
            if (il+1) % c.full_attn_interval == 0:
                st.append({'kind':'attn','k':np.zeros((0,c.n_head_kv,c.head_dim),np.float32),
                           'v':np.zeros((0,c.n_head_kv,c.head_dim),np.float32),'pos':0})
            else:
                st.append({'kind':'gdn','S':np.zeros((c.n_v_heads,c.ssm_state,c.ssm_state),np.float32),
                           'conv':np.zeros((c.conv_k-1, 2*c.inner),np.float32)})
        return st

    def forward(self, toks, st):
        x = np.stack([self.embed(t) for t in toks])
        for il in range(self.cfg.n_layer):
            if st[il]['kind'] == 'gdn':
                x = self.gdn(x, il, st[il])
            else:
                x = self.full_attn(x, il, st[il])
            x = self.ffn(x, il)
        return x

import numpy as np, itertools, sys, json, time
import nref

ORACLE = "tools/oracle_logits_t1_cpu.bin"
oracle = np.fromfile(ORACLE, dtype=np.float32).astype(np.float64)
def sm(x):
    x = x - x.max(); e=np.exp(x); return e/e.sum()
po = sm(oracle)
def metric(lg):
    lg = lg.astype(np.float64)
    cos = float(np.dot(lg,oracle)/(np.linalg.norm(lg)*np.linalg.norm(oracle)))
    top1 = int(np.argmax(lg)==np.argmax(oracle))
    p = sm(lg)
    kl = float(np.sum(po*np.log((po+1e-30)/(p+1e-30))))
    return cos, top1, kl

m = nref.Model({})
st = m.new_state(512)
base = dict(sign_first=True, mt='Tt', emb_mode='inv', conv_rev=False, kmap='repeat', q_layout='per_head', gate_act='sigmoid', gdn_gate='silu')
results=[]
def run(opts, label):
    m.o = opts
    st = m.new_state(512)
    t0=time.time()
    x = m.forward([9419], st)
    lg = m.logits(x[-1:])[0]
    cos, top1, kl = metric(lg)
    results.append((cos, top1, kl, label))
    print(f"{label:55s} cos={cos:.5f} top1={top1} kl={kl:.4f} t={time.time()-t0:.1f}s", flush=True)

variants = []
for sign_first in (True, False):
    for mt in ('Tt','T'):
        o = dict(base); o['sign_first']=sign_first; o['mt']=mt
        variants.append((o, f"sign_first={sign_first} mt={mt}"))
for name in ('emb_mode','conv_rev','kmap','q_layout','gate_act'):
    vals = {'emb_mode':['inv','none','fwd'],'conv_rev':[False,True],'kmap':['repeat','tile'],'q_layout':['per_head','chunked'],'gate_act':['sigmoid','silu']}[name]
    for v in vals:
        if v == base.get(name): continue
        o=dict(base); o[name]=v
        variants.append((o, f"{name}={v}"))

sel = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv)>1 else 0
if sel==0:
    for o,l in variants:
        run(o,l)
else:
    o,l = variants[sel-1]
    run(o,l)
print("BEST:", sorted(results, reverse=True)[:5])
