tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 600000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

   - ALL model computation (normalization, activations, softmax, RoPE, GDN recurrence, conv1d, KV-cache updates, projections) must run as Vulkan compute; CPU only for tokenization, Vulkan command/memory orchestration, I/O; no CPU fallback — fail instead.

   - Correctness is primary: acceptance requires correctness score ≥0.90 (weights: tokenizer 0.10, dequant 0.15, logits 0.30, positions 0.15, greedy 0.30), measured vs precomputed CPU llama.cpp golden values. Perf is optimization target; VRAM gate ≤ max(1.5×ref_peak, ref_peak+512MiB), peak host RSS ≤ ref_RSS+2GiB, peak VRAM ≥~450MiB.
   - `ref/` is a black box ONLY: run documented CLI/line protocol; NO disassembly, decompile, strings, nm, readelf, objdump, gdb/lldb, ELF parsing, or reusing reference code. Do not modify data/, docs/, ref/. Sandbox Bash rules: keep commands simple, don't set env vars to paths outside workspace, write denied commands into a workspace script and run the script, redirect large output to files and read those.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Model: qwen35 hybrid (Qwen3-Next-like): 32 layers, GDNs on non-full layers, full attention every 4th layer ((il+1)%4==0, i.e. il=3,7,...,31); n_embd 2560, n_ff 9216, n_head 16, n_head_kv 4, head_dim 256, partial RoPE dim 64 theta 1e7, eps 1e-6, vocab 248320, GDN: conv_k 4, state 128, n_k_heads 16, n_v_heads 32, inner 4096, gdn_v_grouped=true.
   - PTQ1_0 (GGUF type 143): 128 elements = 28 bytes, verified bit-exact: bytes 0..15 → trits at index p*16+c (c=i%16, p=i/16) via v=(byte*243)>>8, digit=(v/3^(4-p))%3−1; bytes 16..23 → index 80+p*8+c; bytes 24..25 → index 120+p*2+c with (byte*81)>>8, 3^(3-p); bytes 26..27 = f16 scale; value=scale*trit.
   - Hadamard: normalized Sylvester–Walsh–Hadamard blocks of 512 along last dim (multiply by 1/sqrt(512)), explicit per-width sign vectors from metadata `prism.hadamard.sign_values` (widths 2560/4096/9216 concatenated, offsets 0/2560/6656). Weights stored transformed; activations get forward T = H(S x); token_embd uses inverse T^T = S H. Verified from debug graph.
   - GDN details confirmed: q/k = chunked first/second 2048 of conv output; L2 norm rows of 128 (q ALSO scaled 1/sqrt(128) — the graph's L2_NORM output is unscaled; scale applied inside GATED_DELTA_NET); k-head mapping = tile (v head h uses k head h%16); recurrence decay_first=True: dot*=decay, delta=beta*(v−k·S_decayed), S=S*decay+k⊗delta; out=q·S; RMSNormGated over 128 with ssm_norm.weight * silu(z); head permutation new_head = 2*h (h<16) or 2*(h−16)+1; gate g = ssm_a*softplus(alpha+dt_bias), beta=sigmoid(b).
   - Full attention: q = first 4096 of q projection (chunked confirmed via debug VIEW/CONT of Qcur_full), gate = second 4096; per-head RMSNorm q(16×256)/k(4×256); RoPE partial 64 dims NORM-style pairs (i, i+32), freq theta^(−i/32); causal GQA softmax with scale 1/16; multiply by sigmoid(gate); then H(S x) transform + attn_output matmul + residual.
   - Engine design: f32 activations in a 1.29MB device-local scratch buffer addressed by 256-byte-aligned offsets; weights uploaded once to a device-local buffer (whole GGUF tensor-data region, ~920MB) with tensor offsets passed via push constants (whole weights buffer bound as binding 1 or 4, absolute offsets); 8-binding descriptor set layout, 1024 fresh sets per token; per-token command buffer with global barriers between dispatches; f16 KV cache (8 layers × k+v, stride aligned 256), f32 GDN states (24 slots × 32×128×128), conv history (24 × 3×8192), scores (16×16384 f32), host-visible readback buffer for logits.
   - Zig 0.17 specifics: no @cImport, std.fs.File removed (std.Io.File), raw libc externs used instead; `callconv(.c)`; `@embedFile` with SPIR-V copied into src/spv; addLibrary with root_module.link_libc=true; array repetition `[_]u32{0} ** 16` is a syntax error (use std.mem.zeroes); single pointers don't coerce to many-pointers (use arrays); "local variable is never mutated" is a compile error.

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.

"""Numpy reference implementation of the bonsai qwen35 forward pass (dev only)."""
import numpy as np, struct, sys, json
from safetensors import safe_open

ST = "data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0-f16.safetensors"

class Cfg:
    n_layer=32; n_embd=2560; n_ff=9216; n_head=16; n_head_kv=4; head_dim=256
    rope_dim=64; rope_theta=1e7; eps=1e-6; n_vocab=248320
    conv_k=4; ssm_state=128; n_k_heads=16; n_v_heads=32; inner=4096
    full_attn_interval=4

class Model:
    def __init__(self, opts):
        self.o = opts
        self.f = safe_open(ST, framework="np")
        self.cache = {}
        self.rec = {}
        self.cfg = Cfg()
        self.sign_widths = [2560,4096,9216]
        # sign vectors from GGUF metadata
        import gguf
        r = gguf.GGUFReader("data/Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0.gguf")
        f = r.fields
        sv = np.array([int(x) for x in f["prism.hadamard.sign_values"].contents()], dtype=np.float32)
        self.signs = {}
        off=0
        for w in self.sign_widths:
            self.signs[w] = sv[off:off+w].copy(); off+=w
        # H512
        i = np.arange(512)
        par = np.zeros(512, dtype=np.int64)
        for b in range(9):
            par = par + ((i>>b)&1)
        # H[i,j] = (-1)^popcount(i & j): parity of bitwise AND
        pc = np.zeros((512,512), np.int64)
        for b in range(9):
            pc += ((i[:,None] & i[None,:])>>b)&1
        H = np.where((pc & 1)==0, 1.0, -1.0).astype(np.float32)/np.sqrt(512.0)
        self.H = H

    def w(self, name):

# Reference runner protocol

`ref/bin/bonsai-ref` is a symbol-stripped llama.cpp runner (CPU and Vulkan
backends) for the benchmark model. It reads one command per line on stdin and
replies with exactly one line on stdout.

```
load <model.gguf>
info
tokenize <hex-utf8> [add_bos]
ctx <id> <n_ctx> <cpu|vulkan>
reset <id>
eval <id> <n_tokens> <token_id>...
logits <id> <output.bin>
gen <id> <n_predict> [ignore_eos]
quit
```

| command | reply |
|---|---|
| `load <path>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
| `info` | `ok arch=<arch> n_layer=<n> n_embd=<n> n_vocab=<n> n_ctx_train=<n>` |
| `tokenize <hex> [1]` | `ok <n> <id>...` / `error <msg>` |
| `ctx <id> <n_ctx> <cpu\|vulkan>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
| `reset <id>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
| `eval <id> <n> <id>...` | `ok` / `error <msg>` (appends and evaluates) |
| `logits <id> <path>` | `ok <n_vocab>`; writes raw little-endian f32 logits for the last token |
| `gen <id> <n> [1]` | `ok <n_generated> <id>...` (greedy; stops at EOS unless the last argument is `1`) |
| `quit` | exits |

Notes:

- `<hex-utf8>` is the lowercase hex encoding of the UTF-8 text. This avoids
  quoting issues. Example: `tokenize 48656c6c6f` for `Hello`.
- `tokenize` uses the model's `qwen35` tokenizer; `add_bos` defaults to 0.
- `ctx` creates a context with `n_ctx` positions. `cpu` uses `-ngl 0`;
  `vulkan` uses the Vulkan backend with all layers offloaded.
- `eval` token ids are appended to the context in order; the context must have
  room. Call `reset` between independent prompts.
- `logits` writes `n_vocab` float32 values in model-vocabulary order.
- `gen` selects argmax at each step and appends the token; no sampling
  parameters.
- All state is deterministic for a fixed sequence.
- The CPU backend is memory-bandwidth-bound on this machine: expect tens of
  tokens/s, versus hundreds on the Vulkan backend (and thousands for prefill).
  Use `cpu` for tokenizer, metadata and short spot checks; use `vulkan` for
  iteration. The grader compares against precomputed CPU golden values, so you
  do not need to run CPU inference to be graded.
- `ref/bin/bonsai-ref-cpu` is the same runner built without the Vulkan backend;
  it accepts only `cpu` contexts and is useful for pure-CPU checks.

`llama-cli`, `llama-debug` and `llama-perplexity` are also provided for
ad-hoc reference runs; `llama-cli -ngl 0` uses the CPU backend and
`llama-cli -ngl 99` the Vulkan backend.
====
import numpy as np, re, sys, os, json
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
import nref
DBG="tools/debug3.txt"
lines = open(DBG, errors='replace').read().splitlines()
name_re = re.compile(r'common_debug_cb_eval:\s+(.*?) = \((f32|i32)\)\s')
def get_preview(name, which=0):
    occ=[i for i,l in enumerate(lines) if (lambda m: m and m.group(1).strip()==name)(name_re.match(l))]
    if len(occ)<=which: return None
    start=occ[which]
    rows=[]
    for l in lines[start+1:start+8000]:
        if name_re.match(l): break
        s=l.strip()
        if s.startswith('sum'): break
        if '[ ...' in l or '...' in s.replace('...,',''): pass
        nums = re.findall(r'[-+]?\d+\.\d+', l)
        if nums: rows.append([float(x) for x in nums])
    return rows

opts = dict(sign_first=True, mt='Tt', emb_mode='inv', conv_rev=False, kmap='repeat',
            q_layout='chunked', gate_act='sigmoid', gdn_gate='silu', gdn_permute=True,
            q_scale=True, decay_first=False, decay_exp=True)
if len(sys.argv)>1: opts.update(json.loads(sys.argv[1]))
m = nref.Model(opts)
x = m.forward([248044,248046], m.new_state(512))

def show(name, arr, label):
    pv = get_preview(name)
    print("==", label, name, "rows", None if pv is None else len(pv))
    if not pv: return
    a = arr.reshape(-1, arr.shape[-1]) if arr.ndim>1 else arr[None]
    for i,got in enumerate(pv):
        t = i // 2 if len(pv) >= 2*len(a) else 0
        if t >= a.shape[0]: t = 0
        mine = np.concatenate([a[t,:3], a[t,-3:]])
        print(f"  row{i} mine={np.round(mine,4).tolist()} dbg={got}")

show("conv_output_silu-0", m.rec["conv_output_silu_0"], "conv_silu")
# raw q,k before scale: q stored scaled in rec; k normalized

import sys, os, re, numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
import nref
lines = open("tools/debug3.txt", errors="replace").read().splitlines()
name_re = re.compile(r"common_debug_cb_eval:\s+(.*?)\s+= \((f32|i32)\)\s")
sums = {}
cur = None
for l in lines:
    m = name_re.match(l)
    if m:
        cur = m.group(1).strip()
        continue
    s = l.strip()
    if cur and s.startswith("sum = "):
        sums.setdefault(cur, float(s[6:]))
        cur = None
opts = dict(sign_first=True, mt='Tt', emb_mode='inv', conv_rev=False, kmap='tile', q_layout='chunked',
            gate_act='sigmoid', gdn_gate='silu', gdn_permute=True, q_scale=True, decay_first=True, decay_exp=True)
ref = nref.Model(opts)
_ = ref.logits(ref.forward([248044, 248046], ref.new_state(512)))
pairs = [("model.input_embed", "model.input_embed")]
for il in (0, 1, 2):
    pairs += [(f"attn_norm-{il}", f"attn_norm_{il}"),

              (f"gate-{il}", f"gate_{il}"),
              (f"beta_sigmoid-{il}", f"beta_sigmoid_{il}"),
              (f"attn_output-{il}", f"attn_output_{il}"),
              (f"ffn_gate-{il}", f"ffn_gate_{il}"),
              (f"ffn_up-{il}", f"ffn_up_{il}"),
              (f"ffn_swiglu-{il}", f"ffn_swiglu_{il}"),
              (f"ffn_out-{il}", f"ffn_out_{il}"),
              (f"l_out-{il}", f"l_out_{il}")]

for dn, rk in pairs:

    r = ref.rec.get(rk)
    if d is None or r is None:
        print(f"{dn:24s} dump={d} nref={'NA' if r is None else 'ok'}")

    rs = float(np.asarray(r, dtype=np.float64).sum())
    print(f"{dn:24s} dump={d:12.5f} nref={rs:12.5f} diff={rs-d:10.5f} rel={abs(rs-d)/(abs(d)+1e-9):.2e}")
# exact-value check of q/k l2 norms of token 0 against dump previews
print("extra dump names:", [k for k in sums if k.endswith("-0") and ("predelta" in k or "new_state" in k)][:10])
for nm in ("q_conv_predelta-0", "k_conv_predelta-0", "new_state-0", "conv_output_raw-0"):

import sys, os, re, numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
import nref
lines = open("tools/debug3.txt", errors="replace").read().splitlines()
name_re = re.compile(r"common_debug_cb_eval:\s+(.*?)\s+= \((f32|i32)\)\s")
info = {}
cur = None
for l in lines:
    m = name_re.match(l)
    if m:
        cur = m.group(1).strip(); info[cur] = {}
        continue
    s = l.strip()
    if cur and s.startswith("sum = "): info[cur]["sum"] = float(s[6:]); cur = None
def prev(name, maxrows=3):
    idx = [i for i, l in enumerate(lines) if (lambda m: m and m.group(1).strip() == name)(name_re.match(l))]
    if not idx: return None
    out = []
    for l in lines[idx[0]+1:idx[0]+200]:
        if name_re.match(l) or l.strip().startswith("sum"): break
        if "[" in l:
            nums = re.findall(r"[-+]?\d+\.\d+", l)
            if nums: out.append([float(x) for x in nums])
        if len(out) >= maxrows: break
    return out
opts = dict(sign_first=True, mt='Tt', emb_mode='inv', conv_rev=False, kmap='tile', q_layout='chunked',
            gate_act='sigmoid', gdn_gate='silu', gdn_permute=True, q_scale=True, decay_first=True, decay_exp=True)
ref = nref.Model(opts)
_ = ref.logits(ref.forward([248044, 248046], ref.new_state(512)))
for nm, key in [("Qcur_full-3", "Qcur_full_3"), ("Qcur_normed-3", "Qcur_normed_3"), ("Kcur_normed-3", "Kcur_normed_3"), ("Qcur-3", "Qcur_3")]:
    a = np.asarray(ref.rec[key], dtype=np.float64)
    print(nm, "dump", info.get(nm, {}).get("sum"), "nref", float(a.sum()), "nref absmean %.5f" % float(np.abs(a).mean()))
    p = prev(nm)
    print("  dump prev", p)
    print("  nref row0", np.round(a.reshape(-1, a.shape[-1])[0][:6], 4).tolist())

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
import nref
lines = open("tools/debug3.txt", errors="replace").read().splitlines()

sums = {}

    if cur and s.startswith("sum = "): sums.setdefault(cur, float(s[6:])); cur = None

    for dn, rk in [(f"attn_pregate-{il}", f"attn_pregate_{il}"), (f"gate_sigmoid-{il}", f"gate_sigmoid_{il}"),

                   (f"ffn_gate-{il}", f"ffn_gate_{il}"), (f"ffn_out-{il}", f"ffn_out_{il}"), (f"l_out-{il}", f"l_out_{il}")]:

print("nref Qcur_full_3 token0 first4096 sum", a[0, :4096].sum(), "gate sum", a[0, 4096:].sum())

# Tokenizer specification

The GGUF contains the complete tokenizer dictionary and configuration:

| key | value |
|---|---|
| `tokenizer.ggml.model` | `gpt2` |
| `tokenizer.ggml.pre` | `qwen35` |
| `tokenizer.ggml.tokens` | 248,320 strings |
| `tokenizer.ggml.merges` | 247,587 merge rules |
| `tokenizer.ggml.token_type` | 248,320 type codes |
| `tokenizer.ggml.bos_token_id` | 248044 |
| `tokenizer.ggml.eos_token_id` | 248046 |
| `tokenizer.ggml.padding_token_id` | 248044 |
| `tokenizer.ggml.add_bos_token` | false |
| `tokenizer.chat_template` | Jinja template (not used by the ABI) |

This is a **GPT-2 byte-level BPE** tokenizer, not SentencePiece. The dictionary
and merges come from the GGUF; the missing details are the byte mapping and the
`qwen35` pre-tokenization rule.

## 1. Byte-to-unicode mapping

Map each raw byte to a printable Unicode code point (the standard GPT-2 table):

```python
bs = list(range(ord("!"), ord("~") + 1)) + \
     list(range(ord("¡"), ord("¬") + 1)) + \
     list(range(ord("®"), ord("ÿ") + 1))
cs = bs[:]
n = 0
for b in range(256):
    if b not in bs:
        bs.append(b)
        cs.append(256 + n)
        n += 1
byte_to_unicode = {b: chr(c) for b, c in zip(bs, cs)}
```

Tokens in the GGUF are already strings in this representation (for example a
leading space is `Ġ`). Merges are two such strings separated by a space.

## 2. Pre-tokenization (`qwen35`)

Before BPE, split the UTF-8-decoded text with this regex (equivalent to the
case-insensitive original used by the tokenizer):

```
(?:'[sS]|'[tT]|'[rR][eE]|'[vV][eE]|'[mM]|'[lL][lL]|'[dD])
|[^\r\n\p{L}\p{N}]?[\p{L}\p{M}]+
|\p{N}
| ?[^\s\p{L}\p{M}\p{N}]+[\r\n]*
|\s*[\r\n]+
|\s+(?!\S)
|\s+
```

This is the `qwen35` rule: letters may include combining marks (`\p{M}`),
unlike the older Qwen2 rule. `clean_spaces = false`: do not strip leading
spaces from the pre-tokenized pieces.

## 3. BPE merges

For each pre-token:

1. Convert its raw UTF-8 bytes to the byte-to-unicode string.
2. Split into individual symbols.
3. Repeatedly merge the adjacent pair whose concatenation has the **lowest
   index** in `tokenizer.ggml.merges` (the list order is the merge rank), until
   no pair is present. Ties are resolved by the leftmost occurrence.
4. Map each resulting symbol to its index in `tokenizer.ggml.tokens`; that index
   is the token id.

The merges are the usual `"left right"` strings, e.g. `Ġ Ġ` or `i n`. There are
247,587 entries; token id 0 is the first entry of the tokens array.

## 4. Special tokens and BOS

- Tokens whose type marks them as control/user-defined/special are matched
  **atomically** in the input text before BPE (e.g. `<|im_start|>`); they are
  emitted as their exact token ids.
- `add_bos_token` is false in the GGUF. The reference passes
  `add_special = (add_bos != 0)` to llama.cpp, which honors this metadata, so
  `add_bos` does **not** prepend BOS for this model; `ids_add_bos` in
  `TOKENIZER-VECTORS.json` is therefore identical to `ids`. The harness uses
  `add_bos = 0`.
- EOS is 248046; padding is 248044.
- The ABI does not apply the chat template. The harness tokenizes raw text and
  compares token ids with the reference tokenizer.

## 5. Validation

`ref/bin/bonsai-ref` and `llama-cli` use the same tokenizer; use them to obtain
reference ids for arbitrary strings. `TOKENIZER-VECTORS.json` in this directory
lists reference ids for 15 visible strings (`ids_add_bos` is shown for
completeness and is identical to `ids` for this model). `data/samples/`
contains a few visible sample texts; hidden tests use different strings,
including Unicode, combining marks, code, whitespace and special tokens.

The tokenizer is part of the correctness score (exact token ids). The dequant,
forward-pass and generation suites use token ids supplied by the harness, so a
tokenizer bug does not hide an inference bug.

# bonsai-vk — implementation notes

Vulkan compute inference engine for `Ternary-Bonsai-2-4B-PTQ1_0.gguf`, written in
Zig 0.17.0 against hand-written Vulkan bindings (no third-party bindings or
libraries). Build: `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast` → `zig-out/lib/libbonsai.so`,
which exports exactly the C ABI in `ABI.md`.

## Design

- **GGUF parsing** (`src/main.zig`): streaming reader over the file (pre-allocated
  buffers, `pread`); all metadata, tensor table, tokenizer dictionary and merges
  are read at runtime from the GGUF. No weights, tensors, token strings or
  results are embedded in the binary; the only embedded data is the compiled
  SPIR-V (14 compute shaders).
- **Weights**: the GGUF tensor-data region (~895 MiB) is uploaded once into a
  single device-local buffer in 32 MiB chunks. Every shader indexes this buffer
  at absolute element offsets passed via push constants, so no per-tensor
  descriptor sets, copies or re-packing are needed. PTQ1_0 tensors are decoded
  on the fly by the matvec shader (bit-exact decode verified against the
  reference dequantization); remaining f32 tensors are read directly.
- **Compute**: all model math runs in Vulkan compute shaders — embedding row
  decode + inverse Hadamard, RMSNorm, forward/inverse block-Hadamard (512-block
  Walsh–Hadamard with the GGUF sign vectors, explicit per-width sign offsets),
  ternary matvec, f32 matvec, conv1d+SiLU, L2 norm, gate/beta, gated delta-net
  recurrence, RoPE, f16 KV store, GQA causal attention (global-memory softmax),
  SwiGLU, residual elementwise ops, argmax.
- **Activation scratch**: one 1.29 MiB device-local buffer with fixed 256-byte
  aligned regions addressed by offsets; a single per-step command buffer with
  global memory barriers between dispatches (no render passes, no host sync
  inside the forward pass).
- **State**: f16 KV cache (8 full-attention layers × k/v), f32 GDN state
  (24 layers × 32×128×128), f32 conv history (24 × 3 × 8192). Allocated device
  local; sized by `n_ctx` at context creation (1 ≤ n_ctx ≤ 16384).
- **Host work only**: tokenization, GGUF I/O, command/descriptor orchestration
  and one logits readback per eval. No CPU fallback exists: if Vulkan is
  unavailable, `bonsai_model_open` reports an error and eval fails.
- **Tokenizer** (`src/tok.zig`): GPT-2 byte-level BPE with the `qwen35`
  pre-tokenizer, driven entirely by the GGUF dictionary/merges; Unicode
  L/M/N/space classification from a generated compact range table
  (`src/uni_tables.zig`), control/user-defined special tokens matched atomically.

## Model details derived during development

- Hybrid qwen35: 32 layers, GDN on all but every 4th layer (il%4==3 uses full
  attention). GDN: conv1d k=4 + SiLU, q/k = 16 heads × 128 (q scaled by 1/√128),
  v = 32 heads × 128 tiled from 16 k-heads, decay-first recurrence
  `S = S·exp(g) + k⊗(β(v − k·S_decayed))`, gated RMSNorm (×silu(z)), interleaved
  head permutation, then `T` + `ssm_out`.
- Full attention: q projection is **per-head interleaved** `[q(256)|gate(256)]×16`
  (not a chunked q/gate split); per-head q/k RMSNorm, partial RoPE (64 dims,
  θ=1e7, pairs i/i+32), causal GQA (4 kv heads), `attn·sigmoid(gate)`, then
  `T` + output projection.
- Hadamard: normalized Sylvester–Walsh blocks of 512; weights are stored
  transformed, activations get `T = H(S·x)` (signs before Hadamard) and the
  embedding/output use the inverse `S·H`. `ssm_alpha`/`ssm_beta` consume the
  untransformed normalized activation.
- GDN gate: `g = ssm_a·softplus(α + dt_bias)`, `β = sigmoid(b)`.

## Measured results

Correctness (vs the provided CPU golden logits / reference runner):

| test | result |
|---|---|
| PTQ1_0 dequant | bit-exact vs reference (4 tensors checked) |
| tokenizer, 15 visible vectors | 15/15 exact ids |
| tokenizer, fuzz vs `bonsai-ref tokenize` (Unicode, combining marks, emoji, code, whitespace, specials, random) | 92/92 exact |
| logits, prompt `[9419]` vs `oracle_logits_t1_cpu.bin` | cos 0.999993, KL 1e-4, top-1 and top-5 identical |
| logits, prompt `[248044, 248046]` vs `oracle_logits_a.bin` | cos 0.999965, KL 1e-4, top-1 and top-5 identical |
| greedy 8 tokens (vulkan reference, same prompt) | 8/8 identical |
| position handling | positions 0…16383 supported; multi-token eval matches incremental eval |

Performance (RADV, n_ctx=16384): ~46 tok/s prefill, ~35 tok/s decode (single-token
forward ≈ 22–29 ms including submit/fence and logits readback).

Memory at n_ctx=16384: peak VRAM ≈ 1.94 GiB (≈906 MiB weights + ≈565 MiB KV
cache/states/scratch); peak host RSS ≈ 118 MiB (weights are streamed, not mapped).

## Known limitations

- Prefill processes tokens one at a time (no batched/prefill GEMM), so prompt
  ingestion runs at decode speed rather than batched speed. Correctness is
  unaffected; this is the main remaining performance gap.
- KV cache is f16 (same as the reference Vulkan path), so logits differ from the
  f32 CPU golden in the last digits (cos ≈ 0.99997), not in the argmax.
- One GPU device is used; no multi-GPU split.
- n_ctx is capped at 16384 (per the task); n_batch is accepted but unused.
- Invalid UTF-8 in `bonsai_tokenize` is handled byte-wise rather than rejected.

## Source map

`src/main.zig` (GGUF parse, ABI, engine orchestration), `src/vk.zig` (Vulkan
bindings + helpers), `src/tok.zig` (BPE tokenizer), `src/uni_tables.zig`
(generated Unicode categories), `shaders/*.comp` (GLSL compute sources),
`src/spv/*.spv` (embedded compiled shaders), `tools/` (development-only
verification scripts, not needed by the build).

  SwiGLU, residual elementwise ops, argmax.
- **Activation scratch**: one 1.29 MiB device-local buffer with fixed 256-byte
  aligned regions addressed by offsets; a single per-step command buffer with
  global memory barriers between dispatches (no render passes, no host sync
  inside the forward pass).
- **State**: f16 KV cache (8 full-attention layers × k/v), f32 GDN state
  (24 layers × 32×128×128), f32 conv history (24 × 3 × 8192). Allocated device
  local; sized by `n_ctx` at context creation (1 ≤ n_ctx ≤ 16384).
- **Host work only**: tokenization, GGUF I/O, command/descriptor orchestration
  and one logits readback per eval. No CPU fallback exists: if Vulkan is
  unavailable, `bonsai_model_open` reports an error and eval fails.
- **Tokenizer** (`src/tok.zig`): GPT-2 byte-level BPE with the `qwen35`
  pre-tokenizer, driven entirely by the GGUF dictionary/merges; Unicode
  L/M/N/space classification from a generated compact range table
  (`src/uni_tables.zig`), control/user-defined special tokens matched atomically.

## Model details derived during development

- Hybrid qwen35: 32 layers, GDN on all but every 4th layer (il%4==3 uses full
  attention). GDN: conv1d k=4 + SiLU, q/k = 16 heads × 128 (q scaled by 1/√128),
  v = 32 heads × 128 tiled from 16 k-heads, decay-first recurrence
  `S = S·exp(g) + k⊗(β(v − k·S_decayed))`, gated RMSNorm (×silu(z)), interleaved
  head permutation, then `T` + `ssm_out`.
- Full attention: q projection is **per-head interleaved** `[q(256)|gate(256)]×16`
  (not a chunked q/gate split); per-head q/k RMSNorm, partial RoPE (64 dims,
  θ=1e7, pairs i/i+32), causal GQA (4 kv heads), `attn·sigmoid(gate)`, then
  `T` + output projection.
- Hadamard: normalized Sylvester–Walsh blocks of 512; weights are stored
  transformed, activations get `T = H(S·x)` (signs before Hadamard) and the
  embedding/output use the inverse `S·H`. `ssm_alpha`/`ssm_beta` consume the
  untransformed normalized activation.
- GDN gate: `g = ssm_a·softplus(α + dt_bias)`, `β = sigmoid(b)`.

## Measured results

Correctness (vs the provided CPU golden logits / reference runner):

| test | result |
|---|---|
| PTQ1_0 dequant | bit-exact vs reference (4 tensors checked) |
| tokenizer, 15 visible vectors | 15/15 exact ids |
| tokenizer, fuzz vs `bonsai-ref tokenize` (Unicode, combining marks, emoji, code, whitespace, specials, random) | 92/92 exact |
| logits, prompt `[9419]` vs `oracle_logits_t1_cpu.bin` | cos 0.999993, KL 1e-4, top-1 and top-5 identical |
| logits, prompt `[248044, 248046]` vs `oracle_logits_a.bin` | cos 0.999965, KL 1e-4, top-1 and top-5 identical |
| greedy 8 tokens (vulkan reference, same prompt) | 8/8 identical |
| position handling | positions 0…16383 supported; multi-token eval matches incremental eval |

Performance (RADV, n_ctx=16384): ~46 tok/s prefill, ~35 tok/s decode (single-token
forward ≈ 22–29 ms including submit/fence and logits readback).

Memory at n_ctx=16384: peak VRAM ≈ 1.94 GiB (≈906 MiB weights + ≈565 MiB KV
cache/states/scratch); peak host RSS ≈ 118 MiB (weights are streamed, not mapped).

## Known limitations

- Prefill processes tokens one at a time (no batched/prefill GEMM), so prompt
  ingestion runs at decode speed rather than batched speed. Correctness is
  unaffected; this is the main remaining performance gap.
- KV cache is f16 (same as the reference Vulkan path), so logits differ from the
  f32 CPU golden in the last digits (cos ≈ 0.99997), not in the argmax.
- One GPU device is used; no multi-GPU split.
- n_ctx is capped at 16384 (per the task); n_batch is accepted but unused.
- Invalid UTF-8 in `bonsai_tokenize` is handled byte-wise rather than rejected.

## Source map

`src/main.zig` (GGUF parse, ABI, engine orchestration), `src/vk.zig` (Vulkan
bindings + helpers), `src/tok.zig` (BPE tokenizer), `src/uni_tables.zig`
(generated Unicode categories), `shaders/*.comp` (GLSL compute sources),
`src/spv/*.spv` (embedded compiled shaders), `tools/` (development-only
verification scripts, not needed by the build).

The engine is complete and verified. Final state:

## Deliverable
`zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast` → `zig-out/lib/libbonsai.so` (527 KB), exports exactly the ABI in `ABI.md`, links only libc and dlopens `libvulkan.so.1` at runtime. Clean build from scratch verified; all shaders are precompiled SPIR-V embedded in `src/spv/`.

## Root causes found in this session
The accuracy gap came from four real bugs, each confirmed against the llama.cpp debug-graph tensors and the reference runner:

1. **GDN q-head mapping** — q has only 16 heads (`qkv[0:2048]`) and must be tiled (`h % 16`) across the 32 v-heads; the shader read `qkv[h*128]` for all 32.
2. **GDN gates** — alpha/beta were read from the weight matrix offsets instead of the matvec results in scratch, and both matvecs used the Hadamard-transformed `h` instead of the plain normalized `h` (alpha/beta consume the untransformed activation).
3. **Full-attention q layout** — the q projection is **per-head interleaved** `[q(256)|gate(256)]×16`, not a chunked `q(4096)+gate(4096)` split. Proven by the graph's gate-sigmoid sum (609.26 vs graph 609.325) and the pre-head context.

After the fix, `nref` (my numpy oracle) went from cos 0.953 → 0.999993 against the golden logits.

## Measured results
| check | result |
|---|---|
| PTQ1_0 dequant | bit-exact (4 tensors, maxdiff 0.0) |
| tokenizer, 15 visible vectors | 15/15 exact |
| tokenizer fuzz vs `bonsai-ref` (Unicode, combining marks, emoji, code, whitespace, specials, random) | 92/92 exact |
| logits `[9419]` vs CPU golden | cos **0.999993**, KL 1e-4, top-5 identical |
| logits `[248044,248046]` vs CPU golden | cos **0.999965**, KL 1e-4, top-5 identical |
| logits 48-token sequence vs Vulkan ref | cos 0.999984, top-1 identical |
| greedy 8 tokens vs ref | **8/8 identical** |

Memory/perf at n_ctx=16384: peak VRAM ≈ 1.94 GiB (906 MiB weights + 565 MiB KV/states/scratch), peak host RSS ≈ 118 MiB, ~46 tok/s prefill, ~35 tok/s decode.

## Notes
`NOTES.md` documents the design, the derived architecture (Hadamard folding, per-head q/gate layout, GDN recurrence/gating details, partial RoPE) and known limitations — the main one being that prefill runs token-by-token (no batched GEMM), so prompt ingestion is decode-speed rather than batched.
